extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and policy analysts in development economics, education policy, and political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Quasi-experimental empirical assessment of a mass primary-school construction program (SD INPRES) using cohort-based difference-in-differences, selection-correction, robustness checks, heterogeneity analysis, and mechanism tests to evaluate impacts on schooling choices, religiosity, and political outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection correction using Heckman and Newey
rubrics_metrics.description: Address selection into higher levels of education by applying parametric (Heckman, 1976) and semiparametric (Newey, 2009) selection-correction procedures: first estimate the likelihood of completing a given level of education, then estimate the likelihood of completing Islamic education conditional on reaching that level including selection-correction terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heckman uses the inverse Mills ratio as the correction term; Newey uses a series approximation to the true correction term (implemented here with a cubic polynomial in first-step probabilities based on flexible covariates constructed from quintiles interacted with cohort FE). Key to both is excluding from the second stage at least one variable correlated with grade completion but unrelated to school choice (exclusion restriction). The selection-adjusted estimates identify a local average treatment effect among compliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion restriction for selection models
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an exclusion restriction that predicts grade completion but is otherwise unrelated to Islamic school choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper relies on measures of exposure to a pilot compulsory schooling program in the 1960s (Wajib belajar) rolled out in 35 pilot districts as an instrument/exclusion variable in the first step of the selection-correction procedure; in the first step include interactions of cohort FE with the program's extensive and intensive margins (total teachers and schools allocated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial order selection for series approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the order of the approximating power series in semiparametric correction consistent with Newey (2009) and sample effective size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With an effective sample size of 275 (level of policy variation), Newey implies an upper bound of 3 on the polynomial order; the authors use a cubic polynomial and justify selection based on consistency results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate inference for two-step estimators
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct inference for two-step selection estimators using methods shown to perform well in this context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors conduct inference with a percentile-t bootstrap (Yamagata, 2006), which is shown to work well with two-step selection estimators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioning on graduation to separate composition from choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether increases in religious-school graduation are driven merely by increases in overall education by examining Islamic schooling conditional on graduating at the given level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute shares of Islamic graduation at each education level (primary, junior secondary, senior secondary) to show whether the observed increases are driven solely by more students reaching those levels or by shifts in school choice conditional on graduation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use both standard DID and synthetic DID and compare
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate treatment effects with both standard difference-in-differences and synthetic difference-in-differences and compare results for agreement and exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present panels for both standard DID (panel a) and synthetic DID (panel b) and report consistency across specifications, highlighting any exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-varying cohort analysis and event-study style checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Report cohort-specific outcomes and cohort-specific treatment coefficients to capture dynamics and detect pre-trends or S-shaped exposure patterns across cohorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot cohort-specific Islamic school completion rates for high- and low-exposure districts and plot cohort-specific β from the main estimating equation; look for intuitive dynamic patterns (e.g., shift from elementary to secondary Islamic schools) and absence of systematic pre-trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for district-specific latent potential and pre-period conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for district-specific factors correlated with program intensity and latent potential for the outcome (e.g., Islamic schooling) by including interactions of cohort fixed effects with pre-program measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cohort FE interacted with Islamic schools in 1957 and with proxies for the strength of the Islamic sector prior to treatment; also include interactions of cohort FE with the pilot program margins where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to alternative exposure definitions (adding cohorts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test sensitivity of estimates to alternative definitions of exposed cohorts, for example by adding cohorts to the exposure group to capture one generation of students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors add fifteen cohorts (born 1968–87) to the exposure group and report resulting effect sizes, noting expected larger effects on school choice among these cohorts; report any changes in magnitude or significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address measurement error in outcome data and use validation datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and correct for measurement error in primary survey data (Susenas) by validating with alternative data sources that report schooling type at each level (IFLS) or administrative records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify reasons for under-reporting (e.g., Susenas records only highest graduation level and misses pesantren attendance and dual attendance); treat Susenas-based estimates as lower bounds and validate key patterns using IFLS and administrative enrollment records (Appendix tables/figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for differential allocation / pre-trends in program placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether program (SD INPRES) placement was systematically allocated toward districts with differential pre-existing trends in the outcome of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual event-study evidence (Figure 7) and include interactions of election-year FE with pre-1950s vote shares; find little indication of systematic pre-trends in Islamic school attainment and interpret dynamics cautiously when the earliest post-treatment year (1971) precedes major program rollout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct and test indicators of suspicious electoral data
rubrics_metrics.description: When using historical electoral returns (which may suffer fraud), construct indicators of suspicious support or tallies and test whether these are correlated with treatment intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define suspicious support for the regime (Golkar) if vote share is >1 or >1.5 standard deviations above sample mean in a given year; similarly define suspiciously high vote tallies; test whether districts with greater program construction experienced suspiciously higher or lower support/tallies (they did not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use panel models with pre-treatment controls for political outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate district×election panels for political outcomes and allow for differential trends based on pre-treatment vote shares to mitigate confounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow differential trends based on vote shares for key party blocs in 1955 and 1957 and interpret changes in vote shares (Golkar, PPP) in light of timing of schooling exposure and first voting ages of exposed cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity analysis by gender and policy-relevant events
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore heterogeneous treatment effects by gender and by cohorts differentially exposed to contemporaneous policy changes (e.g., veil ban), interacting treatment with gender and cohort indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split cohorts into those born before and after veil ban exposure (1968–72 vs 1973–87) and interact SD INPRES exposure with gender and cohort indicators to test whether girls exposed to veil ban differentially shifted to Islamic schools; interpret gender-by-cohort interaction magnitudes and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity analysis by baseline ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether baseline district-level religio-political preferences (e.g., 1950s vote share for Islamic parties) moderate treatment effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical vote shares as proxies for conservative ideology and report stronger school-choice responses to treatment in districts with one SD higher support for Islamic parties (e.g., ~50% higher likelihood of attending Islamic schools among exposed cohorts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism tests linking schooling to identity and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Test mechanisms by examining changes in curriculum, language knowledge, religious practices, and indices of piety to connect schooling changes to identity outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document that schools in high-exposure districts increased classroom time for Arabic and decreased Indonesian; show SD INPRES increased Arabic knowledge and various religiosity measures (praying, fasting, Qur’an reading, Friday prayer, sunna prayers, prayer groups, zakat), and construct mean indices to summarize effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intergenerational transmission checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether adult exposures affect family-level investments and children's outcomes (marital sorting, parental Arabic literacy, child Arabic literacy) consistent with vertical cultural transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate whether men/women exposed in childhood more likely to marry Islamic-educated spouses and whether parental exposure increases probability that entire household is Arabic-literate; restrict samples (e.g., Arabic-literate parents) to probe transmission beyond formal schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: consider substitution and equilibrium responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret program impacts in the context of market-level and equilibrium responses (e.g., Islamic sector building new schools as substitutes rather than being crowded out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence of new Islamic school construction, curriculum differentiation, and long-run enrollment to argue that religious schools absorbed excess demand for secondary schooling and potentially counteracted secular nation-building objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report effect sizes relative to meaningful baselines and consider precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Express estimated effects in percentage terms relative to means and report standard errors/confidence; note when estimates are noisy or imprecise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: each additional INPRES school per 1,000 children associated with a 2.5 p.p. decline in Golkar vote share (relative to 65% mean); report when selection-adjusted estimates are larger but noisier and when subgroup estimates lose statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appendices and supplemental analyses for validation and robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide extensive supplementary tables and figures (appendix) to present alternative specifications, additional controls, placebo tests, and validation exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper references multiple appendix tables and figures (A.2, A.7, A.9, A.12, A.16–A.27) for robustness checks, measurement validation, graphical evidence, and additional descriptive analysis.
